## 11. Visual design spec (enough to reproduce the mockups)

This section captures the look Mark signed off on in the cover, intro, and result mockups. Colours are given as **semantic roles + reference hex (light mode)**; map them to APR's own brand tokens where they exist (especially the accent, which should be APR's brand colour, not the generic blue below), and provide dark-mode equivalents if the site supports dark mode. Art comes from **Streamline** (icons + illustrations, one family; see the session handoff `tmp/handoff-quiz-c-build.md`).

### 11.1 Colour (semantic, not decorative)

Colour encodes one of four meanings. Two temperatures: cool/positive for value, warm for loss.

| Role | Meaning | Tint bg | Strong (text/icon) | Accent/border |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Valuable | "getting more valuable" | `#EAF3DE` (green 50) | `#3B6D11` (green 600) | `#97C459` (green 200) |
| Slipping | "a tool can take this" | `#FAEEDA` (amber 50) | `#854F0B` (amber 600) | `#EF9F27` (amber 200) |
| Context | the "d" answers | neutral panel (`#F1EFE8`) | muted/secondary grey | none |
| Recommendation | the one move | accent tint (`#E6F1FB`) | accent (`#185FA5`) | accent (`#85B7EB`) — **swap for APR brand** |

- **Slipping is amber, never red and never the old drab beige.** Red reads as failure (violates honest-middle); beige reads as flat.
- **The 3 cover steps** use three gentle tints for warmth + sequence: step 1 accent/blue, step 2 green, step 3 purple (`#EEEDFE` bg / `#534AB7` text).
- **Page** = light neutral; **cards** = white; **soft panels** (balance bar, context strip, opt-in) = light-neutral tint.
- Colour is always reinforced by icon + label + position, never colour alone (accessibility, and it survives dark mode / colour-blindness).

### 11.2 Typography

- **Headlines are serif** (the editorial "voice" font): hero ~30px / line-height 1.25 / max ~32ch; result heading ("Here's what I see") ~26px; intro heading ("Before you start") ~20px.
- **Body is sans**, 16px, line-height ~1.6. Card body 13.5–14.5px, line-height ~1.5.
- **Eyebrows/labels** 12–13px, in the section's role colour, sentence case (the mockups used lowercase labels — fine, but sentence case is the safe default).
- **Two weights only: 400 and 500.** No 600/700.
- **Sentence case everywhere.** No Title Case, no ALL CAPS.

### 11.3 Layout + components

- Reading column ~680px, generous whitespace, vertical rhythm 1.5–2rem between major blocks.
- **Cards:** white, 12px radius, 0.5px hairline border, padding ~1rem 1.25rem.
- **Soft panels:** tinted neutral, 12px radius, no border, padding ~1–1.25rem.
- **No gradients, no drop shadows.** Flat surfaces, hairline borders.

Cover (top to bottom): brand row (small mark + "Agile Pain Relief") → serif headline → subhead (secondary, ~52ch) → reassurance line (muted, ~52ch) → **3-step strip** (grid `repeat(auto-fit, minmax(180px, 1fr))`, gap 14px; each card = 40px rounded-10px icon/illustration chip tinted per step, "step N" label in step colour, 15px/500 title, 13.5px secondary one-liner) → **opt-in panel** (tinted; label "Where should I send your result?", email input + primary button "Show me my map" inline/flex, microcopy "No spam. Unsubscribe anytime."). Opt-in is the **hard gate** (section 8).

Intro step: centered card (~44ch, text-align center) → 44px round accent chip with a privacy icon → serif "Before you start" → caveat paragraph (14.5px secondary, line-height 1.65) → primary button "Start the quiz".

Result page (top to bottom):
1. Eyebrow "your result" (13px, accent).

# Handoff: build Quiz C ("Where is the Scrum Master role going in an AI world?") in Astro

For an agent (or Mark) implementing this quiz in the APR Astro site. The copy is already drafted and reviewed; this brief covers how to wire it into the existing quiz engine, where the design diverges from the engine's defaults, and what's still open.

## 1. What this is

A reflective lead-magnet quiz for APR list growth. Individual-level, aimed at the Scrum Master navigating GenAI. It maps the taker's recent weeks into work that's getting *more valuable* versus work that's *slipping away*, then gives one move. It ladders to the GenAI-for-agile-teams course.

This is a **wholesale replacement of the existing `ai-failure-modes` quiz**, not an A/B test. Quiz C takes its place. (An earlier plan to A/B two quizzes has been dropped.)

## 2. Source of record (the copy)

- `OutsideContent/Generated/Quiz C - ScrumMaster Role in an AI World - draft copy.md`
- **Sections 1-3 are current and reviewed** (cover, the 8 questions, the result model). Lift copy from here.
- **Sections 4-5 are STALE** (two worked examples + a 4-email follow-up sequence). They still reflect an earlier 5-question version and old wording ("note-taking"). Ignore them for the build; they get regenerated against the 8-question result later.
- There may still be open CriticMarkup suggestions in the file. Accept/resolve them in Obsidian's Track Changes before lifting final text.

## 3. Target infrastructure (it already exists)

- **Repo:** `/Users/marklevison/Documents/GitHub/APR/agile-pain-relief-astro`
- **Quiz engine:** `src/lib/quiz-engine/` — read `README.md` first, it's the guide. Components: `QuizStepper.tsx`, `ResultCard.astro`, and a gated stepper for capture.
- **Content collection:** `src/content/quizzes/`. Use the existing `ai-failure-modes/index.mdx` as a reference for frontmatter shape (that's the quiz Quiz C replaces; it must keep working on the band-style renderer, see section 5).
- **Schema:** `createQuizSchema` (in `src/lib/quiz-engine/schema.ts`), extended in `src/content.config.ts` with APR fields: `heroHeading`, `heroBody`, `categoriesHeading`, `persuasion`, `submissionTags`, `levelTagPrefix`.
  - Core fields: `title`, `description`, `intro`, `resultsSubtitle`, `sections[]` (id, label, blurb, image), `questions[]` (id, section, text, reveal, `options[]{text, score}`), `sectionLevels[]`, `overallLevels[]`, `randomize`.
- **Capture:** email-only opt-in, gated by Turnstile, POSTs to `/api/newsletter-signup` (the gated stepper), tags applied via `submissionTags` + `levelTagPrefix` (Cakemail). No browser-direct Cakemail form.
- **Results page is stateless** (all computed values live in the URL query string, shareable/bookmarkable).

## 4. Mapping the copy onto the schema

- `title` / `heroHeading`: "Where is the Scrum Master role going in an AI world?"
- `heroBody` / `description`: the subhead.
- `intro`: the reassurance line + the "Before you start" caveat (not a test, nobody sees your answers, answer for the sprints you actually had).
- `sections[]`: propose three, for grouping and optional section scoring:
  - `time` — "Where your time goes" (Q1, Q2, Q3)
  - `coaching` — "Growing the team" (Q4, Q7, Q8)
  - `system` — "The system around the team" (Q5, Q6)
  - (Sections are optional grouping. Quiz C's result is per-answer, so sections mostly help presentation and any section-level framing.)
- `questions[]`: all 8, each with 4 options (a-d) from the draft.

## 5. The scoring model, and generalizing the engine

**Important:** Quiz C is NOT a single-band "you scored X, you're a Y" result. Its result is a per-answer **map** plus one **move**. The engine today only produces band-based results (what `ai-failure-modes` uses).

**Engine work (part of this task, not a Quiz-C special case):** generalize the quiz engine so it supports *both* result styles from the same schema, the existing **band** style and the new **map + move** style, selected per quiz. Design it as a pluggable result-rendering strategy, because more quiz types are coming. Target shape: a quiz declares its renderer in frontmatter (e.g. a `resultStyle: 'band' | 'map-move'` field, defaulting to `band`), and the engine dispatches to the matching results component. `ai-failure-modes` must keep working unchanged on the band renderer. Put the map + move logic (below) behind the new strategy, not hardcoded into a page.

- **Option scores** (used to classify each answer, not to produce a grand total):
  - Most questions: c = 2 (more valuable), b = 1 (mixed), a = 0 (slipping).
  - **Q3 is inverted** (it measures absorbable admin): a = 0 (a big slice of admin, most slipping), b = 1, c = 2 (little admin, freed up).
  - **d options = context, score 0 but flagged as context, NOT a gap** (see section 7).
- **The map** (draft section 3, "Component library"): for each answer the taker picked, render its matching sentence. Answers scoring "more valuable" go in the "getting more valuable" list; answers scoring "slipping" go in the "slipping away" list. Sentences are keyed by (question, chosen option).
- `overallLevels` can optionally drive a light framing line (e.g. "mostly valuable work" / "a real mix" / "a lot is slipping"), but keep it descriptive, never an archetype label.

## 6. The "one move" algorithm (lives in the map + move renderer)

- **Reclaim target** = the biggest slipping answer, priority order: **Q3 (admin) > Q1 a > Q2**.
- **Redirect target** = the weakest coaching answer, priority: **Q4 > Q7 > Q8**, then the systemic ones **Q5 > Q6**. (Coaching leads because it's the real value of the role.)
- Render: reclaim sentence + redirect sentence (templates in draft section 3), then a one-line list of the other slipping slices.
- **Well-positioned fallback:** if little or nothing is slipping and the taker is strong across coaching + systemic, skip reclaim entirely and show the "rare case" copy (go deeper, help others do the same).

## 7. The "d" answers are context, not gaps

The d options encode real-world constraints (part-time SM also coding/testing, no PO worth coaching, hands-on in the team's build). Do **not** count them as neglect. On the results page, name the constraint rather than scoring it against the taker. Example: a part-timer's thin coaching time is contextual, not the same as a full-timer ignoring coaching. This needs explicit handling in the answer-to-sentence mapping.

## 8. Capture + follow-up

- **Email capture is front-loaded and hard-gated: the email is required to START the quiz** (Mark's decision), not captured at the end the way the engine currently does it. Wire the opt-in on the cover / before question 1, using the existing Turnstile -> `/api/newsletter-signup` path. Rationale: transparency (the taker knows up front that an email is involved) and it self-qualifies for higher-intent leads. The engine generalization (section 5) should make capture *position* configurable (start vs end); this quiz hard-codes the start gate.
- Email-only field. Tag submissions with `submissionTags` (e.g. `quiz-c`, `sm-role-ai`) plus `levelTagPrefix`, so the follow-up sequence can segment on the taker's lead move.
- **Follow-up emails:** draft section 5 has a 4-email sequence, but it's stale (5-question era). Regenerate against the 8-question result before wiring. Not required for a first launch of the quiz itself.

## 9. Open decisions for Mark

- **Course name + link:** draft uses the placeholder "Pragmatic AI for Agile Teams". Confirm final name and URL.
- **URL slug** for the quiz (match existing quiz routing, e.g. under `/quiz/...`).
- Whether to use `overallLevels` for a light framing band, or run purely off the per-answer map.
- **Old quiz disposition:** since this is a wholesale replacement, decide whether `ai-failure-modes` is unpublished or removed, and whether its URL should 301-redirect to Quiz C.

## 10. Invariants to preserve (don't let the build erode these)

- No archetype or personality label. Honest-middle (most people land mixed). No invented peer benchmarks or percentages.
- "blocker" in the taker-facing questions and answers; "impediment" in the result copy where Mark is speaking.
- Voice: no emdash, never "delve", avoid "leverage" and hype words; GenAI/LLM rather than a bare "AI" in Mark's own claims about the tools.
- Coaching is the primary redirect target in the move logic; it's the real value of the role.
- The unflattering answer must stay safe to pick, and the result names every slipping slice honestly (it doesn't hide the extras behind the lead one).

content: Lucide icons are free. Any reason not to use them?

message.content: Lucide icons are free. Any reason not to use them?

content.thinking:
Mark is weighing whether to use free Lucide icons instead of his paid Streamline subscription for icons. I'm thinking through the honest tradeoffs here—Lucide is free, open source, consistently designed, actively maintained, and has over 1400 icons available, which covers a lot of ground.

The real tension is that Lucide's minimalist outline style (single weight, 2px stroke on a 24px grid) might clash with Streamline's more detailed, illustrative approach. Mark specifically wanted one cohesive visual system for both icons and illustrations, and mixing a flat line-icon library with richer illustrations could break that unity. Lucide also can't do filled, duotone, or colored variants—it's outline-only—so if the design calls for more visual variety or color to match the illustrations, Lucide hits a wall there.

On the semantic side, Lucide's coverage skews toward generic UI concepts (arrows, files, settings) rather than the specific metaphorical needs Mark outlined—like distinguishing a "coach" from a "whistle," or representing an "impediment" without it reading as a "no-entry sign." Icons like `ban` or `octagon-x` carry the wrong connotation for his use case. That said, Lucide does offer solid dev ergonomics in Astro with tree-shaking and no licensing friction, and it's free—so if budget or simplicity matters, it's a viable fallback to drop Streamline for icons entirely and use it only for illustrations, or skip both if illustrations aren't critical.

The real tension boils down to visual consistency: pairing Lucide's clean line style with Streamline's richer illustrations creates two distinct visual languages. That works if illustrations stay minimal (like a cover) and icons function as a separate utilitarian layer—a pattern many sites use successfully. Otherwise, committing to all Streamline (icons plus illustrations) keeps everything cohesive but requires the paid investment. The mockup actually used line icons like Tabler, which are visually similar to Lucide, so sticking with Lucide would keep that clean aesthetic without needing illustrations at all. If he's willing to drop the colored cover illustrations and go all-line, Lucide alone solves the problem for free—no need for Streamline. The real trade-off is that Lucide is line-only and single-weight, which limits some design flexibility. coverage for domain-specific concepts like coach, impediment, and product owner — Lucide skews toward UI patterns rather than agile metaphors, so I should verify those icons exist before fully committing. Since he's already paid for a month of Streamline, he could test both systems in parallel and decide which aesthetic works better, then stick with Lucide long-term if it covers everything he needs.

The real choice comes down to whether the final design leans toward rich, colored illustrations or stays minimal and line-based — if it's the latter, Lucide alone is a solid, free solution. I'll hold off updating the handoff docs until he decides, then offer to record the final specs once he's made his call.

content.text:
Lucide's a genuinely good choice, and on its own merits there's no reason to avoid it: human-authored (it's the maintained fork of Feather), very consistent, ~1,500 icons, ISC-licensed for commercial use, and it has a first-class Astro package (`lucide-astro`) that tree-shakes. It's basically Tabler's cousin, and the approved mockup already used line icons, so the quiz would look much like what you signed off on.

The one real reason to hesitate is the thing you bought Streamline for: **consistency with the illustrations.**

- Lucide is **line-only, single weight.** Streamline's *illustrations* are richer and usually coloured. Line icons next to coloured illustrations read as two different visual languages, which is exactly the "one system" look you were after.
- Lucide is **UI/utility-oriented**, so it's thinner on your metaphors. Check your specific concepts before committing: coach-as-a-person, impediment-as-a-barrier (Lucide's `ban` is the no-entry sign you wanted to avoid), Product Owner. It has `users`, `construction`, `target`, etc., but may not nail all your semantic distinctions the way a richer set does.

So the decision really hinges on the cover:

- **If the cover uses rich, coloured illustrations** → keep icons in that same family (Streamline) so they match. Lucide would clash.
- **If you're happy with the clean line look** from the mockup → Lucide is perfect and free, and you'd pair it with either Streamline's *line* illustration style or a minimal/line free illustration set (or skip cover illustrations). In that case you could drop Streamline entirely.

Practical move, since you've already paid for one month of Streamline: use this month to try both side by side. Pull the Streamline set, drop Lucide in via `lucide-astro`, and see which reads better on the real page. If Lucide holds up and you go clean-line, keep it free long-term and let the Streamline sub lapse.

Want me to note this open icon decision (Streamline-coloured vs Lucide-line, gated on the cover's illustration style) in the handoff so it's not lost?

content: Do we try and use graphics to illustrate the questions?

message.content: Do we try and use graphics to illustrate the questions?

content.thinking:
Mark is asking whether to add illustrations alongside each quiz question. Looking at his setup—eight behavioral questions with a clean, utilitarian icon style and a pragmatic brand voice—this feels like a genuine design tradeoff between visual interest and maintaining that honest, no-nonsense aesthetic.

The case for illustrations is straightforward: they'd break up the text-heavy form feel and add warmth. But the case against is stronger here. These are reflective questions meant to prompt real thinking about past sprints, and decorative illustrations risk distracting from that introspection rather than supporting it. Plus, sourcing eight bespoke illustrations consistent with his current Lucide approach would reintroduce the design system friction he just solved by sticking with line icons. One focused question per screen feels like the right call for this kind of reflective work.

The graphics that actually earn their place are the cover (setting tone), the results visualization (making the map legible), and maybe a small Lucide icon per question as a quiet visual anchor without competing for attention. If the eight questions get grouped into sections, a section header with an illustration could work as a sparing touch. The honest move is to keep the question screens calm and let the graphics do their work elsewhere.

A focused single-question-per-screen layout with generous whitespace and big type is what makes this engaging—the motion and answer-tile design carry the weight, not decoration. And there's a real risk with a reflective quiz: an illustration of someone drowning in tickets next to the admin question could bias the response or feel judgmental, so keeping questions visually neutral protects the honesty of the self-report. The recommendation is graphics on the cover, result, and section headers; question screens stay clean with maybe a small icon if testing shows it helps rather than distracts.

I could mock up a single question screen to show how this works—clean layout with or without a small icon—so he can see the difference before committing to the full design.

content.text:
My honest take: no, not a full graphic per question. Here's the reasoning.

These are **reflective questions**. The whole job of a question screen is to get the taker thinking hard about their actual last sprints. A decorative illustration next to each one competes with that introspection, and worse, it can *prime the answer*. Picture someone drowning in tickets next to the admin question, and you've nudged the honest self-report you worked so hard to protect. Calm and neutral is what makes the recall trustworthy.

Two more reasons it's not worth it:

- **It undercuts credibility.** Illustrated-every-question is the BuzzFeed register. Your quiz earns trust by feeling like an honest diagnostic, not a personality-test toy.
- **It reintroduces the consistency problem you just dodged.** Lucide is line icons, not illustrations. Per-question art would need Streamline or similar, and now you're back to matching two families across 8 screens.

Where graphics genuinely earn their place, and where I'd put the effort instead:

- **The cover** (hero + the 3-step strip). Yes, illustration here sets the tone. Already decided.
- **The result** (the balance bar, the iconned lists). Yes, visuals there aid comprehension of the map.
- **Section headers**, if you group the 8 into "time / coaching / system". A single illustration or icon at each section break is a good, sparing use, and it breaks the monotony without touching the questions themselves.
- **At most, a small quiet Lucide icon per question** as an anchor. Optional, and only if it helps rather than distracts.

The real fix for "questions feel like a form" isn't decoration, it's the **flow**: one question per screen, big type, generous whitespace, nicely designed answer tiles, and a little motion between questions (the Typeform move). That's where the engagement comes from.

Want me to mock a single question screen, clean one-per-screen, so you can see it with and without a small icon and decide?

content.text:
That's the whole toolkit for making a text question attractive without any graphics. What's doing the work:

- **One question, a lot of room.** The screen holds a single question on a soft panel with generous padding, so it reads as a calm moment, not a form field.
- **A serif question, large.** The editorial voice font makes the question feel considered and human rather than clinical.
- **Answer tiles, not radio buttons.** Full-width tappable rows with a lettered chip, hairline borders, and rounded corners. Big, forgiving targets that feel good to click, especially on mobile.
- **A clear selected state.** Option b is shown selected (accent border, tint fill, the chip flips to accent) just to demo the feedback, it doesn't imply a right answer. That moment of "yes, got it" is most of what makes a quiz feel alive.
- **Progress + section label.** "1 of 8" and a slim bar give momentum and cut abandonment; the "where your time goes" eyebrow quietly groups the questions.
- **Motion carries the rest.** Selecting auto-advances with a slide/fade to the next question (the Typeform move), so there's no Next button cluttering the screen, just "back" and a soft hint.

So the engagement comes from rhythm, type, tile design, and the selection feedback, not decoration. It stays credible and calm, which is what a reflective quiz needs.

Reactions? Things you might weigh: whether the answer tiles should auto-advance or need a Next button, whether the section eyebrow helps or you'd drop it, and the selected-state colour (that accent should become your APR brand colour in the real build).
